extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, graduate students, historians/philosophers of mathematics, and educated general readers interested in the practice and culture of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the tools, institutions, epistemic limits, and evaluative problems of mathematical practice (how mathematics is done, communicated, preserved, and judged). Useful for readers seeking standards and norms governing mathematical research, education, and dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruments of writing and duplication are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: To do mathematics one must have, at the very least, instruments of writing or recording and of duplication; mathematics is not done totally in the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses the Archimedes-in-the-sand image but rejects the notion that mathematics can be done entirely mentally. Before printing there were 'scribe factories' for wholesale replication. Practical mathematical activity therefore requires recording and copying technology; lack thereof constrains transmission and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean geometry as ruler-and-compass constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: The ruler and compass are built into the axioms at the foundation of Euclidean geometry; Euclidean geometry can be defined as the science of ruler-and-compass constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a definitional/axiomatic standard: what constructions and methods count as legitimate in classical Euclidean geometry is determined by the ruler-and-compass model, which shapes both pedagogy and what is considered acceptable demonstration in that subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic aided historically by external instruments (abacus, slide rule, computer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic has been aided by many instruments and devices; three of the most successful have been the abacus, the slide rule, and the modern electronic computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical succession of aids matters for evaluating methods and expected skills. As computers became available, rote arithmetic became less central and the logical/algorithmic aspects gained prominence; this shift affects training and what practical competence is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computers as indispensable assistants for applied mathematics (numerical & symbolic)
rubrics_metrics.description: To the applied mathematician, working with scientists and engineers to get numerical answers to practical questions, the computer has been an indispensable assistant; when programmed appropriately it can also perform many symbolic mathematical operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: computers handle numerical simulations, formal algebra, formal calculus, series expansions, differential-equation manipulations. However, expected aids (e.g., FORMAC or MACSYMA) did not immediately become universally transformative; practical utility depends on program maturity and suitability to the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer graphics produce mathematically defined objects with no real-world existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer graphics show beautifully shaded and colored pictures of 'objects' which are only mathematically or programmatically defined; the viewer might mistake them for photographs even though the 'objects' have no real-world existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual fidelity of computer-generated images can mislead about physical realizability. In some cases, building a physical model (scaled, color-coded, etc.) is still more effective for understanding complex structures; choose modeling method according to the goal (intuition, verification, communication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of computers shifts research toward constructive and algorithmic results
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrival of a generation familiar with computing has caused greater interest in constructive and algorithmic results and decreasing interest in purely existential or dialectical results that have little or no computational meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computing availability 'lures' mathematicians toward areas where computation plays a role; this affects what problems are pursued and which results gain attention. See further discussion (referenced chapter) for implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most mathematical research continues independent of computers
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite computer advances, most mathematical research continues to go on just as it would have if the computing machine did not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overgeneralize computer impact: while important in many areas, a large portion of pure mathematics remains conceptually or methodologically independent of computational tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics knowledge scope and Ph.D. benchmark (educational prerequisites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate for Ph.D. candidates: ~14–18 undergraduate semester courses and ~16 graduate courses; roughly one book per course and additional collateral reading leads to about 60–80 volumes — 'two shelves' suffice as a basic personal library for a specialist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This offers an educational benchmark for expected background depth. It also highlights serial dependence among subjects (e.g., differential equations requires calculus and linear algebra), which shapes curriculum design and assessment of preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics is cumulative but subject to obsolescence and loss
rubrics_metrics.description: While mathematics builds on itself and prior truths remain in principle, processes also break down earlier structures: individual facts may be erroneous, theories become unpopular, formulations are recast and may become unintelligible; physical records can be destroyed or chemically deteriorate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating historical or older mathematical work, check for reformulation, completeness, relevance, and possible errors; preservation issues (war, paper quality) mean that archival availability and condition affect what can be relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ulam's dilemma: impossibility of global importance judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The enormous and rapidly growing number of theorems published yearly makes it impossible for any one person to survey the field and judge what is 'important'; there are no stated criteria permitting evaluation across widely separated fields of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate global evaluation requires synthesizing judgments from many experts; absent such synthesis and stated cross-field criteria, assessments of importance devolve to local/community standards or market-like mechanisms (publication/refereeing rates), which may not reflect considered value judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding and area-choice procedural norm: deference to market/refereeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Spokesmen for federal funding agencies explicitly deny attempting to evaluate or choose between one area of mathematics and another; if more proposals are made in area X and are favorably refereed, then more will be funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural principle implies that resource allocation follows proposal volume and peer-refereeing outcomes rather than top-down prioritization; it warns that democratic or market-driven funding lacks the debate and deliberation idealized in other decision contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics perpetuated via international forums (meetings, journals, books)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous regional, national, and international meetings are held; lively activity in writing and publishing of books at all levels; more than 1,600 individual technical journals serve as appropriate outlets for mathematical material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation in meetings and publication in appropriate journals and books are the standard means of communicating, critiquing, and validating mathematical work. Choosing the right forum and engaging in the community discourse are implicit standards for dissemination quality.
